Find the total area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y=\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{6}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }({\operatorname{arctan}⁡\frac{x}{6}|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡0-\operatorname{arctan}⁡\frac{a}{6}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡\frac{a}{6} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the total area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y=3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}$ and the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x
$$

We start by calculating the first of these integrals:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x
$$

We calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u={x}^{3}$,  then $\text{d}u=3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.$ Hence, the antiderivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={e}^{u}+C \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{({e}^{{x}^{3}})|}_{a}^{0} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{0}-{e}^{{a}^{3}}) \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We break up the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We start by calculating the second of these integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u=1+{x}^{2}$,  then $\text{d}u=2x\text{d}x.$ Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{2}{{u}^{3}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\frac{4x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }({-\frac{1}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}|}_{0}^{a}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}+\frac{1}{(1+0)^{2}}) \\  & =-0+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{4|x|}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x
$$

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let  $u=3+{x}^{2}$,  then $\text{d}u=2x\text{d}x.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{u})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2(3+{x}^{2})}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now evaluate the first of the improper integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{(-\frac{1}{2(3+{x}^{2})})|}_{a}^{0} \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{2(3+0)}-\frac{1}{2(3+{a}^{2})}) \\  & =-(\frac{1}{6}-0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **odd** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's sketch a graph of the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222009/assets/2b7b85dd8894c73275816a8ee08a8c8a41fb41a327d20ed7bedc489f7e2e55ff.png)

We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x
$$

We start by calculating the first of these integrals:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x
$$

We calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u={x}^{2}$, then $\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x.$ Hence, the antiderivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{u}{3}))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x & =-{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{(\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}))|}_{a}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{{a}^{2}}{3})) \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}(0-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x=\frac{\pi }{12}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}+\frac{\pi }{12} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$
